subject: chemistry-hl
topicLabel: R2.1 How much? The amount of chemical change
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

items.topicLabel: R2.1 How much? The amount of chemical change
items.stem: What is the coefficient of O₂ when the equation is balanced with whole numbers? __C₃H₈ + __O₂ → __CO₂ + __H₂O
items.note: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. Balance C, then H, then O last: 3 × 2 + 4 = 10 O atoms = 5 O₂.

items.topicLabel: R2.1 How much? The amount of chemical change
items.stem: In the reaction N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, how many moles of NH₃ form from 6.0 mol of H₂ with excess N₂?
items.note: Mole ratio H₂ : NH₃ = 3 : 2, so 6.0 × 2/3 = 4.0 mol.

items.topicLabel: R2.1 How much? The amount of chemical change
items.stem: The limiting reactant is the reactant that:
choices: Has the smallest mass at the start of the reaction
Has the smallest coefficient in the balanced equation
Is left over when the reaction has finished
Is completely used up and so decides the amount of product
items.note: Compare moles divided by coefficients, not masses. The reactant left over is in excess.

items.topicLabel: R2.1 How much? The amount of chemical change
items.stem: What mass of iron can be made from 16.0 g of Fe₂O₃ (M = 159.70 g mol⁻¹)? Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ (Ar Fe = 55.85)
items.note: n(Fe₂O₃) = 0.1002 mol → n(Fe) = 0.2004 mol → 0.2004 × 55.85 = 11.2 g. Missing the 1 : 2 ratio gives 5.60 g.

items.topicLabel: R2.1 How much? The amount of chemical change
items.stem: 0.100 mol of Al reacts with 0.100 mol of Cl₂: 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃. Which statement is correct?
choices: Al is limiting and 0.100 mol of AlCl₃ forms
Cl₂ is limiting and 0.100 mol of AlCl₃ forms
Neither is limiting and 0.150 mol of AlCl₃ forms
Cl₂ is limiting and 0.0667 mol of AlCl₃ forms
items.note: Al would need 0.150 mol Cl₂; only 0.100 is present, so Cl₂ limits. n(AlCl₃) = 0.100 × 2/3 = 0.0667 mol.

items.topicLabel: R2.1 How much? The amount of chemical change
items.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 4.00 g. The student obtains 3.20 g. The percentage yield is:
items.note: % yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100 = 3.20 ÷ 4.00 × 100 = 80.0%. A yield above 100% points to an impure (e.g. wet) product.

items.topicLabel: R2.1 How much? The amount of chemical change
items.stem: What is the atom economy for making ethanol by fermentation? C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ (M: glucose 180.18, ethanol 46.08)
items.note: Atom economy = mass of desired product ÷ total mass of reactants × 100 = 2 × 46.08 ÷ 180.18 × 100 = 51.1%. Remember the coefficient 2.

items.topicLabel: R2.1 How much? The amount of chemical change
items.stem: 10 cm³ of methane reacts with 30 cm³ of oxygen: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l). What is the final gas volume at room temperature?
items.note: Gas volumes react in the mole ratio. 10 cm³ CH₄ uses 20 cm³ O₂ (10 left) and makes 10 cm³ CO₂; liquid water has negligible volume. Total 20 cm³.

items.topicLabel: R2.1 How much? The amount of chemical change
items.stem: 25.00 cm³ of 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ Na₂CO₃ needs 21.30 cm³ of HCl for neutralisation. Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. What is the concentration of the HCl?

items.topicLabel: R2.1 How much? The amount of chemical change
items.stem: A student's percentage yield of a crystalline product is 108%. The most likely reason is:
choices: Some product was lost when it was transferred
The reaction did not go to completion
A side reaction formed a different product
The product was not completely dry when weighed
items.note: Over 100% means extra mass: water or another impurity in the product. The other three all lower the yield.

items.topicLabel: R2.1 How much? The amount of chemical change
items.stem: Which change increases the atom economy of a process, rather than its percentage yield?
choices: Recovering more product from the filter paper
Choosing a route that makes no by-product
Using an excess of the cheaper reactant
items.note: Atom economy depends only on the balanced equation. Yield depends on how much product you actually isolate.

items.topicLabel: R2.1 How much? The amount of chemical change
items.stem: 2.43 g of magnesium is added to 100.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid. Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. Determine the limiting reactant and the amount of H₂ formed. (Ar Mg = 24.31)
markscheme: Mg needs 0.200 mol HCl, so HCl is limiting (1)
items.tactic: Limiting reactant: divide each amount by its coefficient; the smaller value limits.

items.topicLabel: R2.1 How much? The amount of chemical change
items.stem: Distinguish between percentage yield and atom economy.
markscheme: Percentage yield = actual mass obtained compared with the theoretical maximum (depends on the practical) (1)
Atom economy = proportion of reactant mass that ends up in the desired product (depends on the equation) (1)
items.tactic: Distinguish = one clear difference per side, in matched terms.

items.topicLabel: R2.1 How much? The amount of chemical change
items.stem: Explain why a process with 100% yield could still be wasteful, and why chemists consider atom economy when designing a green synthesis.
markscheme: A 100% yield can still produce a large mass of by-products (1)
Low atom economy means much of the reactant mass ends up as waste (1)
High atom economy uses resources efficiently / less waste to treat (1)
items.tactic: Green chemistry questions want both the definition and the consequence.

items.topicLabel: R2.1 How much? The amount of chemical change
items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) A student heated 1.000 g samples of an invented metal carbonate, XCO₃, to constant mass: XCO₃(s) → XO(s) + CO₂(g). Results: trial 1 residue 0.562 g; trial 2 0.565 g; trial 3 0.559 g.
(a) Calculate the mean mass of CO₂ lost. (b) Calculate the molar mass of XCO₃ and suggest the identity of X. (c) Explain the effect on the result if heating was stopped before constant mass.
markscheme: (a) Mean residue 0.562 g, so CO₂ lost = 0.438 g (1)
(c) Less CO₂ lost, so fewer moles calculated and M too high (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
